title: Canada Border Services Officer Recruitment 2026
metaDescription: Canada Border Services Officer recruitment 2026: CBSA trainee program, Rigaud training, eligibility, bilingual requirements and officer pay explained.
headline: Canada Border Services Officer Recruitment 2026: Training and Careers

sections.title: The CBSA officer trainee program
sections.content:
Canada Border Services Agency officers work at airports, land border crossings, marine ports and postal facilities, enforcing customs, immigration and agriculture laws. New officers enter through the Officer Trainee Developmental Program, which begins with an 18-week residential course at the CBSA College in Rigaud, Quebec, covering legislation, search and examination techniques, firearms and defensive tactics, and officer safety.

Trainees are paid during training and must pass all evaluations to graduate, after which they are posted to ports of entry across Canada. Officers must be willing to relocate, work shifts including nights, weekends and holidays, and carry a firearm and other defensive equipment as part of their duties.

sections.title: Eligibility and bilingual requirements
sections.content:
Applicants must be Canadian citizens or permanent residents, hold a secondary school diploma or equivalent, and possess a valid driver's licence. They must pass a security clearance, a medical assessment and a psychological evaluation, and meet the physical standards for the role. Prior experience in law enforcement, the military or customer service is an asset but not a requirement.

Many officer positions are designated bilingual, requiring English and French at the BBB level or higher, and bilingual candidates receive priority for those posts. Applicants who are not yet bilingual can still be hired for unilingual positions, and the CBSA offers language training for officers who wish to qualify for bilingual roles later in their careers.

sections.title: Pay, progression and daily work
sections.content:
Border services officers earn a starting salary of roughly C$75,000 or more, rising with experience and through the FB officer pay scale, with overtime, shift premiums and bilingual bonuses adding to total compensation. Officers progress from trainee to fully qualified officer and can advance to senior officer, superintendent and chief positions, or specialise in areas such as intelligence, investigations, detector dog handling and marine operations.

Daily work varies by posting: airport officers interview travellers and examine baggage, land border officers process vehicles and commercial shipments, and marine officers board vessels. All officers must exercise sound judgement, since their decisions on admissibility and seizures can be reviewed by tribunals and courts, and integrity is treated as a core requirement of the job.

faqs.q: How long is CBSA officer training?
faqs.a: New officers complete an 18-week residential course at the CBSA College in Rigaud, Quebec, covering legislation, search and examination techniques, firearms and defensive tactics, and officer safety. Trainees are paid during the course and must pass all evaluations to graduate, after which they are posted to ports of entry across Canada.

faqs.q: Do you need to be bilingual to join the CBSA?
faqs.a: Not for every position, but many officer posts are designated bilingual, requiring English and French at the BBB level or higher, and bilingual candidates receive priority for those roles. Unilingual positions exist, and the CBSA offers language training for bilingual posts. Communication skills matter for all officers.

faqs.q: What salary do Canada Border Services Officers earn?
faqs.a: Border services officers start at roughly C$75,000 per year or more, rising with experience through the FB officer pay scale. Overtime, shift premiums and bilingual bonuses add to total compensation, and officers receive federal public service benefits and pension. Senior officers, superintendents and specialists earn significantly more as they advance.

Officers work at international airports, land border crossings, marine ports and postal facilities across Canada, processing travellers, vehicles and commercial goods. After training, officers must be willing to relocate to their assigned port of entry and work shifts including nights, weekends and holidays. Postings change over a career as operational needs evolve.
